frames.narration: The user types an email and a password. The edge checks the address and the device. It is a known phone on a familiar network, so the risk score is low and no CAPTCHA is needed. The request is passed on.

The login service loads the user's salt and stored argon2id hash, computes the hash of what was typed with the same salt and settings, and compares in constant time. This takes about 100 ms of one CPU core, which is why attack traffic must be filtered before this step.

The password is right but it is only one factor. The login service asks for the second factor. The phone signs a fresh challenge with its passkey. The signature covers the real site's origin, so a look-alike phishing site could never obtain one that works here.
Both factors passed. The token service creates a signed access token valid for 10 minutes and a random refresh token r1, and stores only the hash of r1 in a new family for this device.
The login, the risk result and the factor used are written to the audit log, which is shipped to a separate store and cannot be edited by the services.

The phone calls an API with the access token. The API checks the signature with the public key and the expiry. There is no call to the login service or a database, so this scales with the number of API servers.

Ten minutes later the access token has expired. The phone presents r1. The token service sees that r1 is unused, marks it used, and issues a new access token and a new refresh token r2 in the same family.

Someone had copied r1 earlier and now tries to use it. It is already marked used, which can only happen if two parties hold it. The token service revokes family F1, including r2, so the thief is stopped, the real user must sign in again, and an alert is raised.
